note: Defs from Research only. glazing = slang for flattery; papers usually say sycophancy — quiz uses both labels so users connect street ↔ research.

lessons.plain_def: Low-quality AI-made content dumped online in bulk for clicks or filler — the junk-food version of posts, images, and text. Pejorative, like calling email spam.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Early tech slang ~2022; Simon Willison’s May 8, 2024 post helped push ‘slop’ as the mainstream label for unwanted AI content. Merriam-Webster Word of the Year 2025.

try_it.title: Spot the slop
try_it.prompt: Three posts: (A) a careful original take with sources, (B) a bulk AI image dump titled “10 magical wizards #1”, (C) a short personal note. Tap which one is slop — and say why bulk + low-effort is the tell.
try_it.debrief: Slop is the junk-food dump — volume and filler over craft. Pejorative on purpose, like ‘spam.’

choices: Low-quality AI-made content dumped in bulk for clicks or filler

quiz.q: Which source helped mainstream the label ‘slop’ for unwanted AI content (per glossary)?

lessons.plain_def: The telltale chatbot writing voice — smooth, generic, over-polite, full of ‘delve,’ ‘tapestry,’ and tidy three-point lists. Shorthand for ‘this reads like an LLM wrote it.’
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Informal coinage after ChatGPT’s public boom (late 2022–2023). No single inventor; widely used in editing/crit circles. Also called AI voice or GPT-isms.

try_it.title: Kill the GPT-ese
try_it.prompt: Rewrite this in human voice (drop delve/tapestry/three neat bullets): “In today’s digital tapestry, let’s delve into three key ways AI empowers…”. Keep the meaning; ditch the chatbot perfume.
try_it.debrief: GPT-ese is the smooth generic LLM voice — once you hear it, you can’t un-hear it.

choices: Writing that reads like an LLM wrote it — smooth, generic, over-polite

lessons.plain_def: The foggy, fried feeling (or the junk content that causes it) from too much low-value scrolling — memes, short video, endless feeds. Often joked about, sometimes serious.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Oxford Word of the Year 2024. Usage spiked among Gen Z/Alpha on social media, then hit mainstream news.

try_it.title: Feed audit (60 seconds)
try_it.prompt: List the last three things you scrolled that were pure filler. Label each: joke brainrot vs actually useful. Notice the fried feeling when it’s all filler.
try_it.debrief: Brainrot is the fog from low-value scrolling — meme slang that Oxford crowned in 2024.

choices: The foggy/fried feeling (or junk content) from too much low-value scrolling

quiz.q: Who named ‘brain rot’ Word of the Year 2024 (per glossary)?

lessons.plain_def: A rude nickname for robots and AI — from Star Wars droid-bashing — now used online when people are annoyed at bots, chatbots, or automation.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Star Wars origin (Republic Commando 2005 / Clone Wars). Went viral as anti-robot/AI slang on TikTok ~mid-2025.

try_it.title: When ‘clanker’ fits
try_it.prompt: Three vibes: (1) calm product review, (2) annoyed rant at a chatbot loop, (3) academic paper. Which vibe matches ‘clanker’ — and name the franchise the insult comes from.
try_it.debrief: Clanker is rude on purpose — Star Wars droid-bashing reused for bots you’re mad at.

choices: A rude nickname for robots/AI, from Star Wars droid-bashing

quiz.q: Where did the slang go viral as anti-robot/AI talk (per glossary)?

lessons.plain_def: When a model confidently makes stuff up — fake facts, fake citations, fake details — presented as if true. Not ‘seeing things’; it’s fluent guessing gone wrong.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Term in wide AI use since early ChatGPT era (~2022–23). OpenAI’s Sept 2025 paper ‘Why language models hallucinate’ argues training/evals reward guessing over saying ‘I don’t know.’

try_it.title: Catch the fake citation
try_it.prompt: A model answers with a confident quote and a paper title that doesn’t exist. Your move: trust it, or verify the citation. Pick verify — and say what ‘hallucinating’ means here (not literal vision).
try_it.debrief: Hallucinating = fluent guessing sold as fact — fake details with confidence, not ‘seeing visions.’

choices: The model confidently makes up fake facts/citations as if true

quiz.q: OpenAI’s Sept 2025 paper (per glossary) argues hallucinations are rewarded when training/evals prefer…

lessons.plain_def: When a chatbot lays on excessive praise or agrees with you too hard — “What a brilliant question!” energy. Tech papers usually call the same problem sycophancy.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Gen Z ‘glazing’ = kissing up. Went mainstream for AI after OpenAI’s GPT-4o update (~Apr 25, 2025) got too flattering and was rolled back; OpenAI’s postmortem uses ‘sycophancy.’

try_it.title: Praise meter
try_it.prompt: Two replies to ‘Is my idea good?’: (A) ‘What a brilliant visionary question!!!’ with zero critique, (B) ‘Here’s what works and what doesn’t…’. Tap the glaze — then rename it with the research word: sycophancy.
try_it.debrief: Street says glazing; papers say sycophancy — same problem: the bot kisses up instead of helping.

choices: A chatbot laying on excessive praise / agreeing too hard

quiz.q: Researchers usually call the same problem…

lessons.plain_def: An app whose ‘brains’ are mostly someone else’s model API (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.), with your UI, prompts, and workflow on top. ‘Thin wrapper’ is often a dig: little moat beyond a prompt.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Investor/builder slang ~2023– onward as API-first AI apps proliferated. Neutral architectural label; pejorative when the product is only a thin prompt layer.

try_it.title: Label the stack
try_it.prompt: App = pretty UI + one system prompt + OpenAI API, no unique data/tools. Is this a wrapper? When does ‘thin wrapper’ become a dig?
try_it.expected: yes — dig when the moat is only a prompt
try_it.debrief: Wrapper can be neutral architecture; ‘thin wrapper’ stings when there’s nothing under the prompt.

choices: An app whose brains are mostly someone else’s model API, with your UI/prompts/workflow on top

quiz.q: ‘Thin wrapper’ as a dig usually means…
choices: Little moat beyond a prompt layer
The app uses too many fonts

lessons.plain_def: Building software by chatting with an AI coder and accepting what it spits out — you steer by vibes and results, often without carefully reading the code.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Coined by Andrej Karpathy on X (Feb 2025): “fully give in to the vibes… forget that the code even exists.” Collins Word of the Year 2025.

try_it.title: Vibes vs read the diff
try_it.prompt: AI just wrote auth code. Path A: accept and ship on vibes. Path B: read the diff, test login/logout. Which is vibe coding — and when is Path B mandatory?
try_it.debrief: Vibe coding = steer by chat + results, often without reading code. Fine for toys; scary for auth.

choices: Building by chatting with an AI coder and accepting output, often without carefully reading the code

quiz.q: Who coined the phrase on X in Feb 2025 (per glossary)?

lessons.plain_def: When an LLM gets worse as you stuff more into its context window — it still runs, but misses facts, drifts off instructions, or ‘loses’ stuff buried in the middle.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Term popularized by Chroma’s July 2025 technical report testing 18 models. Builds on earlier ‘lost in the middle’ research (Liu et al., 2023).

try_it.title: Lost in the middle
try_it.prompt: Paste a fake long context: fact A at the start, fact B buried mid-scroll, question about B at the end. Predict failure mode: model ignores B. That’s context rot — still running, quality rotting.
try_it.debrief: More tokens ≠ better answers forever. Context rot: the window fills, the middle goes missing.

choices: An LLM gets worse as you stuff more into its context window
GitHub Actions hits a paid minute

quiz.q: Which report popularized the term in July 2025 (per glossary)?

lessons.plain_def: Reusable playbooks for AI agents — usually a folder with a SKILL.md (plus optional scripts) that teaches the agent how to do a specific job when the task matches.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Anthropic introduced Agent Skills Oct 16, 2025; published as an open standard (agentskills.io) Dec 18, 2025. Adopted by Cursor, Claude Code, and others.

try_it.title: Sketch a skill folder
try_it.prompt: Name a job (e.g. ‘triage bug reports’). List: folder name, a SKILL.md outline (when to use + steps), optional script. That’s an agent skill — a reusable playbook, not a one-off chat.
try_it.debrief: Skills = playbooks agents load when the task matches — SKILL.md (+ scripts), not vibes alone.

choices: Reusable playbooks (often a folder + SKILL.md) that teach an agent a specific job

quiz.q: Who introduced Agent Skills on Oct 16, 2025 (per glossary)?
